generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology gives you plenty to revise actively across all three families. A visual mind map can link a theory to its supporting and contradicting studies; reading an evaluation aloud exposes the gaps in your argument; and walking through the stages of a research method anchors the sequence. The strongest revision in psychology combines families, because a theory you can both diagram and explain aloud is one you can deploy under exam pressure.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students revise the same difficult topic: the working memory model, with its several linked components.

Tom makes one neat set of written notes and reads them over each day. The notes are accurate and tidy, but he never leaves one family: it is all reading. The components blur together, because nothing forces him to reproduce the model or say it aloud. One passive technique, repeated, is still passive.

Amara draws the model as a labelled diagram, then explains each component aloud into a recording, then lays a card for each component around her desk and rehearses how they interact while moving between them. Three techniques from three families, each demanding a different kind of production. The diagram fixes the structure, the spoken version catches her gaps, and the physical layout anchors how the parts connect. This is a varied, active approach.

Both revised the model for the same time. Amara chose techniques across families that matched the material, and ended with knowledge she could retrieve by more than one route.
generatedProse.summary: Active revision techniques in psychology come in three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. You can now distinguish them and say what each suits, evaluate which turn a passive task active, and select a mix across families for a given topic. What unites the strong choices is production: rebuilding, explaining or enacting a theory rather than merely reviewing it. The final lesson takes your prepared knowledge into the exam itself.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's revision more active than Tom's?

items.text: She used techniques from several families, each forcing her to produce the model in a different way.
She made neater and more accurate notes than Tom.
She spent longer revising than Tom.
She read her single set of notes more often.

feedback.correct: That's right. Drawing on several families, each demanding production, is what made it active.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about producing the model across more than one family.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara used techniques from several families, each forcing a different kind of production. Neater notes, more time or more re-reading would all have stayed passive.
